asBirthCard.p: Ten's a funny number. It's the last one you can count on your fingers and the first that needs two digits, a one with a nought after it, so an ending and a fresh start are written in the same spot. That's where your birthdate lands. Add up every digit of it, keep adding while the total's over 22, and yours comes to ten, either straight away or by way of 28, 37, 46 or 55. None of your signs come into it. The Hermit sits just before this card, a man alone up a mountain with a lantern. Then the Wheel, where everything's moving again. There's a snake going down one side, something with a jackal's head coming up the other, and a sphinx on top. After the Wheel comes Justice, who weighs up what the turning did. The Wheel belongs to Jupiter, the planet that makes things bigger, so on this card the good years tend to be very good and the bad ones go further down than you'd like.

Mostly it shows up as a life with chapters you can name. Someone at a party asks how you ended up in your line of work and the answer has a twist in it, a job you took because a friend dropped out, a flat you got because the other applicant moved to Perth. You notice when something's come round again. It's March and you think, hang on, it was March last time the money went sideways too. On a Sunday with nothing planned you're fine for about an hour, and then you're looking at flights or moving the couch to the other wall, because a completely flat week makes you itchy. And when a message turns up from someone you haven't heard from in six years, it doesn't surprise you much. People drift back into your life. You half expect it.

Luck is the gift everyone mentions with this card. The one underneath it is that you're very good company for someone who's hit the bottom. A friend's marriage ends or their business goes under, and most people either go quiet or start handing out advice. You sit down with them and talk about the time it happened to you, how long it took, what came after, and they believe you because you've actually been there, usually more than once. The same thing makes you steady when a workplace gets restructured or the family business has a terrible year. You've watched things drop and come back, so you don't panic, and the people around you borrow some of that calm without quite knowing where it came from. A lot of the time you're the first person they ring when the next thing goes wrong.

The less obvious trouble is what you do when things are going well. Calm can feel a bit suspicious to a ten. The job's good, the relationship's fine, the rent's paid, and some part of you starts waiting for the drop, and now and then, to be honest, you give the wheel a shove yourself so at least you picked the moment. You quit the good job. You start a fight on a quiet weekend. Jupiter's in there too, and in a good stretch it makes you generous in ways that cost later, the round of drinks for the whole table, the bigger lease, saying yes to three projects because you can't imagine ever being tired. Then the turn comes and you're stretched thin. When you catch yourself getting twitchy in a calm patch, ask what you're actually bracing for.

When something goes wrong, the first thing you usually do is move. You make a big call fast, cut your hair, put the car up for sale, start looking at houses in another town, because doing anything feels better than sitting at the bottom waiting. A week later the adrenaline's gone and the second phase kicks in, which is going over it again and again for the exact moment it turned, the email you should have sent, the sign you missed. You start reading meaning into small things. For the people around you the hard part is the whiplash. Your partner agreed to the big change on Monday, and by Friday you're wondering aloud if it was a mistake. What helps is holding off for a fortnight on any decision you can't undo, and keeping the ordinary things going, the same breakfast, the same walk, the Thursday call with your sister.

You often meet people when you're in between things, after a move or a breakup or a new job, and the relationship gets tied up with that phase of your life. Which is lovely until the phase ends. The job changes or you move again, and you catch yourself wondering whether the relationship belonged to the old life, when really it's just the first time the two of you have had to be ordinary together. Partners who need things steady can find you a bit hard to settle with, because they can feel you watching the horizon. You keep the dates, too, the first dinner, the night it nearly ended, and bring them up years later, which a partner finds either sweet or a bit unnerving. It helps to tell them plainly when you're in a restless patch, so they don't take it as being about them. Usually it isn't.

You do well in work that runs in seasons, or in cycles you can see coming. Retail and hospitality, events, farming, teaching with its terms, sales with its quarters, anything where the end of the financial year actually matters. You're often good in a turnaround, the shop that's had a bad year or the team nobody wants to take on, because to you a low point is somewhere things start from. Where you struggle is the long flat middle of a project, month nine of eighteen, when nothing's changing and nobody's saying thanks. That's usually when the job ads come out. Money for a ten tends to arrive in waves, fat quarters and thin ones, especially if you work for yourself. In the good months, move a fixed amount into an account you can't see from your banking app, and leave it there for the thin ones.

At twenty a lot happens to a ten that they didn't choose. A parent moves the family interstate, a course gets cancelled, someone leaves. It can feel like being thrown about, and plenty of them go through a stretch of believing they're just unlucky. By the mid-thirties there's usually enough history to see the shape of it, and often a moment of realising that the worst year turned out to be where the good part started. After that most people with this card get calmer about the drops and a bit more careful at the peaks. The fifties often bring a kind of ease. You've been round enough times that neither the top nor the bottom feels personal any more, and the card's Jupiter streak gets generous in steadier ways, a spare room for a nephew between flats, some money behind a younger friend's first go at a business.

Next time you're in a bad patch and lying awake over it, open the calendar on your phone and make an event three months out. Put the worry in the title in plain words, 'money still tight?' or 'are we OK?', and leave it there. When it pops up, read it and see where things actually got to. Do it every time something drops. After a few of them you've got a record, in your own words, of how things really move for you, and it's there to scroll back through on the next bad night.
